text: It is often argued that university education should be free for all students, while others believe that students ought to pay for their own studies. In my view, a partially subsidised system offers the most reasonable compromise. On the one hand, there are strong arguments for free higher education. Firstly, when tuition is free, talented students from poor backgrounds are able to attend university, which means that the country does not waste its human potential. Secondly, graduates generally earn higher salaries and therefore pay more tax during their working lives, so the government eventually recovers its investment. On the other hand, free education is extremely expensive for the state. If the government pays for every student, the money must come from somewhere else, such as healthcare or public transport. In addition, some students may not take their studies seriously if they have not paid anything themselves. In conclusion, although I understand the concerns about cost, I believe that the government should cover tuition for students from low income families and ask wealthier families to contribute. This approach keeps university accessible without placing an impossible burden on public finances.

text: The rapid growth of cities in developing countries has become one of the defining trends of the last fifty years. While this urbanisation has brought undeniable economic benefits, it has also created serious social problems that governments have struggled to address. The economic case for urban growth is straightforward. Cities concentrate labour, capital and infrastructure in one place, which makes businesses more productive and creates employment on a scale that rural areas simply cannot match. A worker who moves from a village to a city typically triples their income within a few years, and the money they send home supports families in the countryside as well. Nevertheless, the speed of this growth has outpaced the ability of authorities to provide basic services. In many cities, informal settlements have expanded far faster than water supplies, sewerage or public transport, with the result that millions of residents live in conditions that damage their health. Traffic congestion and air pollution impose further costs that fall most heavily on the poor. In my opinion, the solution is not to discourage migration, which is both impractical and unfair, but to plan for it. Governments that invest in housing and transport before the population arrives, rather than after, consistently achieve better outcomes than those that simply react to overcrowding.

text: The shift towards remote working has been one of the most significant changes to professional life in recent decades, and opinion remains divided over whether it has improved or damaged working culture. Although the drawbacks are real, I would argue that the benefits substantially outweigh them for most knowledge-based occupations. The most obvious advantage is the elimination of the commute. Employees who previously spent two hours a day travelling now have that time returned to them, which they typically invest in sleep, exercise or family life. The consequences extend beyond individual wellbeing: fewer commuters mean less congestion and lower emissions, benefits that are enjoyed by the wider community rather than by workers alone. Remote arrangements have also widened access to employment for people with disabilities and for those living far from major cities, groups that were previously excluded from many careers. Critics counter that collaboration suffers when colleagues never meet, and there is some justification for this concern. Spontaneous conversation is difficult to replicate over video, and junior staff in particular lose the informal mentoring that comes from sitting beside experienced colleagues. However, these problems stem from poor implementation rather than from remote work itself. Organisations that bring teams together periodically, and that deliberately structure mentoring rather than leaving it to chance, report no decline in either productivity or staff development. On balance, therefore, the evidence suggests that remote work is not a compromise but an improvement, provided that employers are willing to redesign their practices rather than simply relocating the office into the home.

text: Governments facing competing demands on limited budgets frequently question whether the conservation of endangered species deserves public funding at all, particularly when that money could be directed towards housing, healthcare or education. While the moral case for protecting other species is often made, I would argue that the strictly practical case is more persuasive and, crucially, more difficult for sceptics to dismiss. Ecosystems are not collections of independent organisms but tightly coupled systems in which the removal of a single species can trigger consequences far beyond anything anticipated. The near-elimination of wolves from Yellowstone, and the subsequent transformation of its river systems once they were reintroduced, remains the clearest illustration of how indirect these effects can be: a predator was found to be shaping the physical geography of a landscape. Since we are rarely able to predict which species perform such roles until they have disappeared, treating any extinction as an acceptable loss involves a gamble whose stakes are unknown. There is also a straightforwardly economic dimension. A substantial proportion of modern medicines derive from compounds first identified in wild organisms, and the overwhelming majority of species have never been screened for pharmacological activity. Each extinction therefore closes off possibilities that we cannot value precisely because we have not yet examined them. Set against the cost of protection, which is trivial in the context of national budgets, this represents an exceptionally poor trade. None of this is to suggest that conservation should take precedence over acute human need. It is rather to observe that the choice is usually presented as far starker than it actually is, and that the sums involved are small enough that framing the question as conservation versus hospitals obscures more than it reveals.

text: The line graph illustrates changes in the proportion of city residents using three modes of transport, namely buses, private cars and bicycles, over the twenty-year period from 2000 to 2020. Overall, the private car overtook the bus as the dominant mode of transport during this period, while cycling, despite starting from a very low base, was the only mode to grow consistently throughout. In 2000, buses were used by approximately 45 per cent of residents, comfortably ahead of cars at 30 per cent, with bicycles accounting for a mere 10 per cent. Bus use then declined steadily, falling to 35 per cent by 2010 and to just 25 per cent by the end of the period, a loss of twenty percentage points overall. Car use followed the opposite trajectory, rising to 40 per cent in 2010, at which point it overtook the bus for the first time, and reaching a peak of 50 per cent in 2020. Cycling, meanwhile, grew more modestly but without interruption, doubling from 10 to 20 per cent across the two decades. Although it remained the least used of the three modes throughout, by 2020 the gap between cycling and bus travel had narrowed to only five percentage points, compared with a gap of 35 points in 2000.
